newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget pact praised, but next steps difficult.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget pact praised, but next steps difficult.

text.p: The historic bipartisan accord to balance the budget by 2002 reached between President Clinton and the Republican-led Congress now faces months of tough work to win approval of its provisions.

The long-sought budget agreement must clear a Congress whose most conservative members charge its tax cuts are not large enough and whose most liberal Democrats threatened to vote against it due to deep domestic spending cuts. Once the budget blueprint is adopted, separate committees will start working out details of spending cuts and tax cuts.

Negotiators worked feverishly in the 24 hours leading up to the final deal to mute objections. To mollify Democrats, they dropped certain changes in the Medicaid and Medicare health care programmes and Social Security which had been certain to draw fire from liberals.

They also brought key Republicans on board with careful assurances that House and Senate tax committees would be only loosely bound to specific tax cuts as part of the net $85 billion in lower revenues over the next five years.

And, to clinch the deal the Congressional Budget Office late Thursday found a multibillion-dollar cushion of extra money to spend in the five years when it revised its economic forecasts. The buoyant economy has led to a new forecast for this year's deficit of $75 billion down from $127 billion.

Clinton anticipated the difficulties putting the provisions of the budget into law. "No one will look at this budget and say, 'this is perfect'... But I think we've got a good shot at getting a majority of both parties in both houses," he said as he announced the accord at a meeting with Democrats in Baltimore.

Leaders of both parties rallied behind the final plan, which provides tax cuts and slows the growth of federal spending enough to bring the deficit to zero by 2002. But they also noted much work needs to be done before its provisions become law.

"There will be changes along the line but they will have to be changes that stay within the spirit of what we agreed to. We have to work together (with the president)," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott told reporters.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota committed to its passage. "This budget does not contain everything we wanted. But it contains everything we need to eliminate the deficit and prepare for the future," he said.

House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri, who had been cool to the proposed accord a day earlier, said he was "especially pleased" that a potential threat to Social Security was removed when they eliminated a legislative change in the calculation of the Consumer Price Index. The change would have shown up as smaller inflation raises in benefit checks to seniors.

Moderate Democratic Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland, a member of the party's leadership, said he thought a majority of House Democrats would support it. But one key Democrat, liberal Representative Charles Rangel of New York, who is senior on the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, reserved judgment. "The people who benefit from tax cuts are not my constituents," he said.
While voices of objection were drowned Friday by the large middle ground who announced support for the pact, months of tense negotiations on specific changes lie ahead.

This budget accord must be voted on by both chambers of Congress, but it merely directs other committees and is not binding law. It does not go to the White House for the president's signature. Clinton will have the power to veto or sign into law the separate spending bills and tax bills which may not arrive at his desk until fall.

Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer, the chief House tax writer, who had balked at allowing the budget to specify tax rate cuts or tax increases, ultimately praised the agreement. But he noted, "Of course, we must still successfully implement the plan." The work in his committee will be the focus of financial markets and the public for months to come.

At his insistence the agreement was carefully worded to note that it "can accommodate" tax cuts sought by both Republicans and Democrats, but did not direct taxwriters to do so. However, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said it would include a $500 per child tax credit. It was also designed to allow Republicans their priority of a capital gains tax rate cut.

The budget balancing effort was helped by a favourable economic situation that led to a revised forecast of this year's deficit of $75 billion, well below the more than $120 billion forecast at the start of the fiscal year.
